day-1.t: Day 1 — What Google Ads really is, and what it costs

b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand how the auction actually works
Learn the four words you will see on every screen
Decide the most you are willing to pay for one customer

b.v: About 20 minutes. Do this with a pen. The numbers you write today control everything later.

Google Ads shows your ad to people who just typed something. You pay only when someone clicks. It is not magic and it is not a printing press. It is a shop counter: rent per visitor, and you decide whether each visitor is worth the rent.
1) The four words you must know
Every screen in Google Ads uses these. Learn them once and the rest of the interface stops being frightening.

v: Impression = your ad was shown. Free.
Click = someone tapped your ad. This is what you pay for.
CPC = cost per click: the average rupees you paid for one click.
Conversion = the action you wanted, such as a call, a WhatsApp message or an order.

b.v: Add two more you will meet in reports: CTR is clicks divided by impressions, and CPA is cost per conversion, meaning what one customer action cost you.
2) You are bidding, not buying a fixed slot

When someone searches, Google runs an instant auction. Your bid, your ad quality and the landing page all matter. A higher bid does not always win, and a cheap bid can still show if your ad is more relevant.

v: Your maximum bid = the ceiling you set, not always what you pay
Ad quality = how relevant Google thinks your ad and page are to the search
Actual CPC = often lower than your maximum, because you usually pay just enough to beat the next advertiser

b.v: 3) Work out what a customer is worth

This is the only number that keeps you safe. If a repair job earns you Rs 4,000 profit and one in five clicks becomes a job, then a click is worth about Rs 800 to you. Spending Rs 300 per click is fine. Spending Rs 1,500 is not.

Write these four numbers in your notebook:|My average sale in rupees|My profit on that sale, after parts and labour|How many enquiries I need for one sale, roughly|So the most I can pay for one enquiry

Example: a Peshawar furniture shop sells a Sofa set at Rs 85,000 with Rs 18,000 profit. About one in ten WhatsApp enquiries becomes a sale. So one enquiry is worth roughly Rs 1,800, and the shop should aim well below that per enquiry. These figures are illustrative; use your own.
Never start with 'let us try Rs 500 a day and see'. A daily budget without a target cost per enquiry is just a countdown to losing money. Decide the ceiling first.
Practice
Do this now:|Write your four numbers on paper|Write one sentence: 'I will not pay more than Rs ___ for one enquiry'|Stick it near your desk|Note the date. You will compare against it on Day 10

day-2.t: Day 2 — Set up the account without losing control of it

b.v: Today's goal

v: Create an account you own, with billing you understand
Set time zone, currency and billing correctly the first time
Keep a written record of who has access

b.v: About 20 minutes. Some settings cannot be changed later, so read before you press continue.

The account setup screen is where beginners make permanent mistakes. Time zone and currency are locked after creation, and an agency-owned account can leave you with nothing when the relationship ends.
1) Create the account from your own Google login
Use a business Gmail you control, the same one you use for Search Console and your Business Profile. If someone else creates the account, ask for administrator access before any money is spent.

Set up cleanly:|Go to ads.google.com and sign in with your business Gmail|Choose 'Switch to Expert Mode' if offered, so you see the full menu|Enter your real business name and website|Set the time zone to your city and the currency to PKR|Write the login and password in a diary at home
2) Understand what billing asks for

Google will ask for a payment method. Cards are the usual route. Some accounts can pay by bank transfer after a verification period. Prepaid vouchers and wallet transfers are not the same as Google billing, so do not send money to a stranger who promises to 'load' your account.

v: Cards = the normal payment method, charged automatically
Bank transfer = available in some accounts after checks, not instantly
Prepaid = some countries have it; check what your account actually offers
Never = do not give your card to a third party who runs ads 'for' you

b.v: 3) Turn off the extras Google adds by default
During setup, Google offers to widen your targeting and add partners. These are not evil, but they spend money outside search results, which is not what you want in week one.

In settings, check these:|Search partners: off for now|Display Network: off for now|Location options: set to 'people in your targeted locations', not 'interested in'|Automatically created assets: off until you understand them|Ad suggestions auto-apply: off

Do not let a 'Google Ads expert' you met on Facebook create the account in their name and run it for a monthly fee with no access for you. You must be able to log in, see the spend and export the data. Ownership is not a detail; it is the whole thing.
Practice

Do this now:|Create the account and stop at the campaign screen|Screenshot your settings page|Write down: time zone, currency, payment method, who has admin access|Invite one trusted person as admin, not as the owner

day-3.t: Day 3 — Pick a campaign type and build one campaign

b.v: Today's goal

v: Know the three campaign types a beginner should care about
Build one Search campaign with tight structure
Avoid mixing display and search in one campaign

b.v: About 25 minutes. Build it but keep it paused until Day 7.

A campaign is a container: it holds your budget, your locations and your ads. Choosing the wrong type is like renting a billboard when you wanted a shop sign. For a first campaign, Search is almost always right, because it reaches people who typed what you sell.
1) The three types that matter

v: Search = text ads on Google results. Best for people already looking. Start here.
Performance Max = Google's automated mix across Search, YouTube, Display and Maps. Powerful later, opaque for beginners.
Display = banner ads across websites. Cheap clicks, low intent. Not for your first Rs 20,000.

b.v: There are others, such as Shopping for product feeds and Video for YouTube. They work, but each needs its own setup and its own lesson. Learn Search first and you will understand every report afterwards.
2) One campaign, tight groups
Structure keeps your money honest. A campaign holds one budget. Inside it, ad groups hold keywords and ads that belong together, so the ad can match the search.

Build it:|Press New campaign, choose the 'Leads' or 'Sales' goal, then Search|Turn off the 'add broad keywords automatically' suggestions|Name it plainly: Search - AC Repair Lahore - Nov|Set locations to Lahore plus a radius you actually serve|Set language to English and Urdu if your customers use both|Create three ad groups with 5 to 10 keywords each

Example ad groups for an AC repair business in Lahore: 'AC service', 'AC gas refilling', 'AC installation'. Each group gets ads that use those exact words. Someone searching 'AC gas refilling' should not see an ad about installation.
3) Write the settings down
You will forget what you changed. A one-page note saves hours later.
Write in your notebook:|Campaign name and start date|Daily budget|Locations and radius|Bid strategy|Networks on or off|Who changed what, and when

Do not put Search and Display in one campaign because Google offers to 'reach more people'. The clicks come from everywhere, you cannot separate the results, and your search data becomes useless. Keep them apart, or leave Display off.
Practice
Do this now:|Build one Search campaign, paused|Three ad groups, 5 to 10 keywords each|Add your locations and languages|Screenshot the settings page and keep it in a folder called Ads

day-4.t: Day 4 — Keywords and match types, where money leaks

b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand the three match types in plain words
Add negative keywords before you spend a rupee
Build a starter list of 20 to 30 keywords

b.v: About 25 minutes. This is the most important technical lesson in the course.
A keyword is a phrase you tell Google to watch for. A match type tells Google how loosely to match it. Get this wrong and you pay for people searching for jobs, free downloads and second-hand parts.
1) The three match types
Google writes them with symbols, but think of them as strict, medium and loose.

v: Exact match = [ac repair lahore]. Only close variants such as plurals and small misspellings.
Phrase match = "ac repair lahore". Searches that include the meaning of the phrase, in order.
Broad match = ac repair lahore. Anything Google thinks is related. Widest and riskiest.

b.v: For a beginner with a small budget, start with phrase and exact. Broad match can work later, once you have a list of negative keywords and conversion data to guide it.
2) Negative keywords are your seatbelt
A negative keyword tells Google never to show your ad for that word. Add them before launch, not after you notice the bill.
Add these as negatives for a repair business:|free|job|jobs|vacancy|salary|course|training|diy|second hand|used|wholesale|cheap|near me if you do not travel
Think about what your customer is NOT. A clinic does not want 'free', 'government hospital' or 'medical college'. A tailor does not want 'free pattern' or 'sewing machine repair'.
3) Build your first list from real evidence
Do not invent keywords from imagination. Use Google's autocomplete, your own WhatsApp questions, and the free Keyword Planner inside your Ads account for rough volumes.

Build 20 to 30 keywords:|Take the 12 customer questions from your day-to-day chats|Write each as a search phrase with your city|Add the obvious variants: price, cost, near me, service, repair|Group them into your three ad groups|Check each one in Keyword Planner for rough search volume, remembering it is only an estimate
Do not add 200 keywords on day one. You cannot watch them all, and the useless ones quietly eat the budget. Twenty well-chosen keywords with tight match types beat two hundred loose ones every time.
Practice

Do this now:|Put your keywords into the three ad groups|Set phrase or exact match on all of them|Add at least 12 negative keywords at campaign level|Write your list in a notebook so you can compare in a month
Today's goal

v: Write three responsive search ads with real differences
Use the headline space for the offer, not the shop name
Add sitelinks and callouts that earn extra space

b.v: About 20 minutes. Write on paper first. The box on screen makes people write badly.

Your ad is a tiny shop sign: a headline, a description, maybe a phone number. The searcher compares three or four of them in two seconds. The ad that answers the exact question wins the click, even if it is not the cheapest.
1) The parts of a search ad
A responsive search ad asks for up to 15 headlines and 4 descriptions. Google mixes them. You do not control the final combination, so every headline must be able to stand alone.

v: Headline = up to 30 characters. Put the service and city here.
Description = up to 90 characters. Put the reason to choose you and the price signal.
Display path = the two short words after your domain, such as /ac-repair/lahore.
Assets = sitelinks, callouts and call buttons that add extra lines.

b.v: 2) Three ads that say different things
Do not write three ads that all say 'best quality service'. Test three different reasons: speed, price transparency, and trust.

Write one ad per angle:|Speed: 'AC Repair in Lahore Today' / 'Same-day visit, 2-hour slot'|Price: 'AC Service from Rs 2,500' / 'Clear price before we start'|Trust: '12 Years Fixing ACs in Lahore' / '1,000+ homes, 6-month warranty'|Each ad needs at least 8 headlines and 3 descriptions|Pin only the headline that must always show, such as the service name
Prices in ads must be true. If you write 'from Rs 2,500', a visitor must be able to get that price. A bait price is the fastest way to burn money on clicks that never convert.
3) Assets that make the ad bigger
Sitelinks add extra clickable lines under your ad, and they cost nothing extra. They also tell the searcher you have more to offer.

v: Sitelink = extra link such as 'Prices' or 'Areas We Cover'. Add at least four.
Callout = short promise such as 'Free Survey' or 'Same-Day Visit'. Add four to six.
Call asset = a tap-to-call button. Essential if you take phone calls.
Structured snippet = a list such as services or brands.

b.v: Do not use all 15 headlines for keyword variations of the same sentence. If Google combines them, you get 'AC Repair Lahore AC Repair Lahore'. Use the space for different benefits, and check the ad preview on mobile before you save.
Practice

Do this now:|Draft three ads on paper, one per angle|Count characters, since limits are strict|Type them into your three ad groups|Add four sitelinks and four callouts|Read the mobile preview aloud. If it sounds like a robot, rewrite it

day-6.t: Day 6 — The landing page decides whether the click was worth it

b.v: Today's goal

v: Match the page to the ad, word for word
Put price, proof and a contact button above the fold
Give every ad group its own destination

b.v: About 20 minutes. You may only need to edit one page, not build a new website.

A landing page is the page a click arrives on. If the ad says 'AC gas refilling' and the page opens with a company history, the visitor leaves. You paid for that visit and got nothing. The page is half of Google Ads.
1) Message match
The first line of the page should repeat the promise of the ad. This is called message match, and it is the cheapest improvement you can make.

Example: the ad says 'AC Service from Rs 2,500'. The page heading should read 'AC Service in Lahore from Rs 2,500' and the next line should say what happens when they call. Not 'Welcome to our website'.
2) The five things above the fold
Above the fold means the part visible before scrolling on a phone. On a phone that is a small space. Use it well.

v: The offer in plain words, with the price if you can
One proof line, such as years working or number of jobs done
One clear button: WhatsApp, Call, or Book
A photo of real work, not a stock photo of a man in a suit
No menu clutter. On a paid landing page, remove the top menu.

b.v: Fix your page today:|Make the H1 match the ad headline|Move the phone number and WhatsApp button to the top|Delete the pop-up that asks for an email before showing the price|Add one real photo of finished work|Test on your own phone on mobile data, not office wifi
3) Give each ad group its own page

If you have three ad groups, send them to three different pages, or to one page with three clear sections and link to the right section. Sending all traffic to the home page is the most common waste in small accounts.

Do not send paid clicks to a page that takes more than three seconds to load, or to a page with a form that asks for a CNIC and an email address for a simple enquiry. Every extra field costs you enquiries. Ask for name and phone number, nothing more.
Practice

Do this now:|Open each ad group and check where its final URL points|Write one sentence per ad group: what page should this go to?|Fix the H1 on your main landing page to match the ad|Ask one person to find your price in ten seconds on their phone|Note what they did first. That is what your customers do.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Budget and bidding: spending like a business

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set a daily budget you can survive for 30 days
Choose a bid strategy you can understand
Launch small and watch the first week properly

b.v: About 20 minutes. Then launch. A paused campaign teaches you nothing.
Your daily budget is a limit, not a target, and Google can spend up to about twice the daily amount on a busy day while averaging out over the month. Plan the monthly number, not the daily one.
1) Pick a number you can lose
Treat your first month as paid learning. Decide an amount that will not hurt your household or your stock money if it brings nothing.

Example, purely illustrative: a small shop sets Rs 20,000 for the first month, about Rs 650 a day. If clicks cost around Rs 60 to Rs 120 in that market at the time of writing, that is roughly 5 to 10 clicks a day. From that they expect one or two enquiries a day and a handful of sales. Your market and costs will differ, so check the estimates Google shows in your own account before you commit.
2) Bid strategies in plain words

v: Manual CPC = you set the maximum cost per click yourself. Most control, most work.
Maximize clicks = Google spends your budget to get the most clicks. Fine for the first week to gather data, dangerous if left on.
Maximize conversions = needs conversion tracking and some history. It will struggle with no data.
Target CPA = you give a cost per conversion target. Only use once you know your real numbers.

b.v: For week one: Maximize clicks with a maximum CPC cap, or manual CPC. Then move to conversions once tracking has recorded enough. Do not use target CPA on an empty account.
3) Launch checks before you unpause

Go through this list:|Conversion tracking is live, or you accept you are flying blind (see Day 8)|Billing is active and the card works|Locations and languages are right|Negatives are in place|Final URLs open on a phone|Budget is set to the monthly figure divided by 30|Campaign is unpaused and you have 30 minutes to watch it

Do not raise the budget on day two because you are impatient. The first 48 hours mostly show you what Google thinks your ad is about. Changes made in panic usually make the data unreadable and the spend worse.
Practice

Do this now:|Set your monthly number and divide by 30|Choose Maximize clicks with a CPC cap|Run the launch checklist|Unpause|Set a phone reminder for the same time tomorrow to look at the search terms report

day-8.t: Day 8 — Conversion tracking you can trust

b.v: Today's goal

v: Define what counts as a conversion for your business
Set up tracking for calls or WhatsApp, not only forms
Check that the numbers are real, not doubled

b.v: About 25 minutes. This lesson saves more money than any bidding trick.

Without conversion tracking you can see clicks and cost but not results. You then judge ads by CTR, which is like judging a shop by how many people walked past the door. Tracking turns spend into a number you can defend.
1) Choose the conversions that matter
Pick one or two primary actions. Too many conversions makes the data noisy and the automated strategies confused.

v: Primary = the action closest to money, such as a WhatsApp enquiry or a call
Secondary = a useful but weaker step, such as a price page view
Not a conversion = a page visit or a scroll. Those are not results.

b.v: 2) Three ways to track in a small business
Most Pakistani small businesses get their enquiries by phone and WhatsApp. Track those, not just the website form.

Pick the ones you can actually do:|Website tag: install the Google tag on your site, then mark the thank-you page as a conversion|Call tracking: use a Google forwarding number so calls from ads are recorded|WhatsApp clicks: make the button a tracked click and count it as a conversion, then confirm real chats manually
If you use WhatsApp, count the click as a signal and keep a simple paper log of real conversations. The click is not a sale, but it is much closer to one than a page view.
3) Test it before you trust it
A broken or doubled tag gives you confident wrong answers. Spend ten minutes checking.

Test like this:|Open your site on your phone, submit a test enquiry|Wait a few hours, then check the conversions column|If it shows two conversions for one enquiry, the tag fires twice. Fix it.|If it shows none, the tag is missing or on the wrong page|Ask a friend in another city to call the ad number and check it appears

Do not mark a page view as a conversion just to make the account look busy. You will optimise toward people who browse, not people who buy, and the automated bidding will happily spend your budget on them.
Practice

Do this now:|Write down your one primary conversion|Check whether your site has the Google tag installed|Send one test enquiry and find it in the conversions report|Write the date you tested it in your notebook

day-9.t: Day 9 — Read the reports and plug the leaks

b.v: Today's goal

v: Use the search terms report to find waste
Judge keywords by cost per conversion, not clicks
Know the difference between a bad keyword and a bad page

b.v: About 25 minutes. Do this on a laptop. The tables are too wide for a phone.
The search terms report shows the actual phrases people typed before clicking your ad. It is the most honest screen in Google Ads, and the place where most wasted money is visible within a week.
1) Read the search terms report

Do this weekly:|Open Campaigns, then Insights and reports, then Search terms|Sort by cost, highest first|Mark anything irrelevant as a negative keyword|Look for surprising phrases that deserve their own ad group|Note phrases with many clicks and no conversions
Realistic example: a Karachi laptop repair shop finds it paid for 'laptop repair course in Karachi' and 'free laptop repair software'. Both are wasted clicks. Both become negatives in ten seconds.
2) Judge with the right column
Clicks and CTR flatter you. Cost per conversion tells the truth. A keyword with 30 clicks and no enquiries is worse than one with 4 clicks and 2 enquiries.

v: Search impression share = the share of eligible searches where your ad showed. Low share can mean budget or bid limits.
Cost per conversion = spend divided by conversions. Compare it to your ceiling from Day 1.
Conversion rate = conversions divided by clicks.
Quality score = Google's rough 1 to 10 relevance signal. Useful as a hint, not a grade.

b.v: 3) Diagnose before you panic
A keyword with traffic and no conversions has one of three problems. Name it before you act.

Ask in this order:|Is the search term actually what I sell? If no, add a negative.|Does the ad promise the same thing as the page? If no, fix the page.|Is the price simply wrong for this market? If yes, no ad can fix it.|Only then consider pausing the keyword

Do not pause a keyword after three clicks and no sale. Small numbers are noise; a shop can get ten clicks and no sale by chance. Give a keyword enough clicks to be judged, or your account will end up with nothing running and no answers.
Practice

Do this now:|Open the search terms report and sort by cost|Add five negatives|Find one search term worth its own ad group|Write your cost per conversion next to your Day 1 ceiling|Decide one change, and only one, for this week

day-10.t: Day 10 — The 7-day launch plan and the traps to avoid

b.v: Today's goal

v: Follow a seven-day launch plan in order
Recognise the ten ways beginners waste money
Set a weekly routine you can keep

b.v: About 25 minutes. Print the plan and tick each day.
You now know every part. What separates a working account from a leaking one is order and patience: build small, measure honestly, change one thing a week.
1) The seven days

Day 1: write your numbers and ceiling. Create the account, check settings.|Day 2: build one Search campaign, paused, with three tight ad groups.|Day 3: add 20 to 30 phrase and exact keywords, plus 12 negatives.|Day 4: write three ads per group, one angle each, and add sitelinks.|Day 5: fix the landing page H1, price and contact button. Test on a phone.|Day 6: install or verify conversion tracking and send a test enquiry.|Day 7: set the budget, run the checklist, unpause, and book a daily 15-minute check for the next week.
2) The ten leaks

v: Broad match with no negatives
Sending every ad group to the home page
A landing page with no price
Tracking clicks instead of enquiries
Raising budget in panic on day two
Leaving search partners and display on by default
Running ads to a page that takes five seconds to load
Judging after three clicks
Never reading the search terms report
Letting someone else own the account

b.v: 3) Your weekly routine
Fifteen minutes, same day each week. This is the whole job once the campaign is running.

Every week, in this order:|Check spend against the monthly plan|Read the search terms report and add negatives|Look at cost per conversion against your ceiling|Pause anything with enough clicks and zero conversions|Try one improvement: a headline, a negative, a page line|Write one sentence in your notebook about what changed

Also be careful with automated recommendations. Google will suggest raising budgets and widening targeting, because that increases spend. Some suggestions are good. Read the reason, and accept only what matches your own numbers.

Nobody can guarantee a position or a cost per lead. If an agency promises a fixed number of sales for a fixed fee, ask to see the account, the tracking and the reports. Keep admin access, export your data monthly, and never let anyone spend your card without written approval of the budget.
Practice

Finish with this:|Copy the seven-day plan into your calendar as seven events|Do the checklist for your current campaign|Set a repeating weekly reminder for the routine|Write your target: enquiries per month at a cost below Rs ___ each|Check that number on the same date next month, not before
